stories.summary: On the morning of the shoot, Amit's mind wandered while shaving and he cut his lip. The cut kept bleeding, leaving a trail of blood down to his bare torso. Ajay put on his 'scientific hat', said oxygen makes blood clot, and told him to stand in front of a fan. Amit asked if a hairdryer would do, and so became perhaps the first person in history to aim a hairdryer at his lips. He then drew the metaphor: one superficial cut stops bleeding, but a body with a thousand deep cuts and no clotting mechanism just keeps bleeding.
stories.insight: The cold open becomes the frame for the whole episode. India's pension promises are deep cuts with no clotting mechanism, a fiscal haemorrhage that does not heal on its own.
stories.quote: But imagine a body where you have a thousand deep cuts and the mechanism of clotting isn't there, and it bleeds and it bleeds and it bleeds, and what's going to happen, right?

stories.topic: What Kept Jayaprakash Narayan Up at Night
stories.summary: In mid-2023 Amit recorded his third episode with the politician Jayaprakash Narayan. JP told him that one thing kept him up at night, something so big he could not think about anything else: India's pensions crisis, as states moved to replace the NPS with the Old Pension Scheme. Amit had never heard of NPS or OPS and wondered what the fuss was about. JP replied, 'No, Amit, we are destroying our future generation.' That sent Amit to Ajay, who turned out to be one of the architects of the NPS.
stories.insight: The biggest threats to a country are often invisible to smart, well-read people because they hide behind dull acronyms. 'Scheme to scheme' turned out to be a question of generational justice.
stories.quote: He said that there is one thing that keeps me up at night that I'm really worried about, and I think it is so big I cannot think about anything else, and that is our pensions crisis.

stories.topic: From a Port Workers' Whip-Round to Bismarck's Free Promise
stories.summary: Pensions began as small acts of grace. At one port, when workers' health broke from lugging cartons, their fellow workers pooled a little money to support them. Bismarck made it a state affair: in 1889 he announced a pension of 50% of last year's income, payable from age 70. There were no antibiotics, doctors were still putting leeches on patients, and few people lived much past 70. The promise sounded generous but cost almost nothing. Over the next century, rising longevity, falling birth rates and political tinkering turned the same idea into a runaway disaster.
stories.insight: A policy can be easy to announce precisely because its cost is zero today. Its price is hidden in mortality tables and demographics that will flip decades later.
stories.quote: So once again, this was a tiny gesture which feels nice but was not economically material.

stories.summary: By the 1990s, pension payouts for the railways, the military and civil servants were surging. In 1998, under the Vajpayee government, Maneka Gandhi was Minister of Social Justice and Anand Bordia was a joint secretary there. Bordia worked with Gautam Bhardwaj, then at the Invest India Economic Foundation, to set up Project Oasis. It was led by Surendra Dave, founding chairman of SEBI, and Ajay sat on its expert committee. Dave's intuition was that equity returns, modern technology and auction-procured index funds could make a cheap, attractive pension system. Bhardwaj and Dave then calculated the present value of the promises made to civil servants: 68% of GDP, for a tiny sliver of the population. The number reached the 'big four' of the NDA cabinet: Yashwant Sinha, Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee. All four grasped at once that it had to be fixed.
stories.insight: Whoever does the right calculation reframes the debate. People had been alarmed by pension flows that doubled every six years. Seeing the stock as a share of GDP made the problem existential.
stories.quote: That was an eye opener and it helped wake up everybody on the scale of this problem.

stories.summary: Ajay was then in the Ministry of Finance. Vajpayee kept sending back variations: suppose we do it like this, show me the numbers. Finally he settled on a formula. Civil servants would get a 10% wage hike, so 100 became 110, and 20 would be deducted into a personal pension account, leaving take-home pay at 90. Vajpayee judged that this was a fair deal for giving up the old defined-benefit promise.
stories.insight: Good reform is not only technically sound but politically packaged. The 10% sweetener was a statesman's judgement about what people would accept as fair.
stories.quote: Suppose you do it like this, show me the calculations. Suppose you do it like this, show me the calculations, and finally he settled on this that ten, ten and ninety.

stories.topic: 'Yeh To Karna Hi Hai': The Cabinet Meeting
stories.summary: Ajay worked directly with Yashwant Sinha, S Narayan and UK Sinha, and they carried the case up to Jaswant Singh, Advani and Vajpayee. Ajay was not in the decisive cabinet meeting, but UK Sinha was and told him about it. The big four favoured the reform and many other ministers did not. Vajpayee, who had a way of either appearing to be asleep or actually being asleep in meetings, sat with his eyes almost closed and took in the debate. At the end he ruled: 'Yeh to karna hi hai' ('This simply has to be done'). He signed the file on 12 December 2002, and every new central government employee from 1 January 2004 went into the new system.
stories.insight: Reforms with a hundred-year payoff need a leader willing to spend political capital on benefits no current voter will see. Ajay offers Vajpayee's line as a motto for every reformer.
stories.quote: So I want to put up Yeh to karna hi hai as the slogan for every dreamer, every reformer, every do gooder in the country that you have to bite the bullet and you have to do these things.

stories.topic: The 2004 Crash That Steadied the Ship
stories.summary: In the 2004 campaign, a Congress candidate in Delhi tried to stir up anger that the NDA was taking away defined-benefit pensions, but it got no traction. New recruits were fine with the switch. Then on 17 May 2004 the stock market crashed after some CPM politicians talked about tearing the house down. Ajay makes a causal claim: the crash helped Sonia Gandhi settle on Manmohan Singh, Chidambaram, Montek Ahluwalia and C Rangarajan as the economic team, people who had led the reforms all along. The market calmed down, and the new UPA government re-examined the NPS from scratch rather than scrapping it.
stories.insight: A market panic can discipline politics. Here it helped put a reform-minded team in charge at the moment a fragile reform was handed from one government to the next.
stories.quote: This is the dream team of the people that had been leading the reforms all along. So we're in good hands and the stock market rapidly lost its jitters.

stories.summary: While the UPA was re-examining the NPS, Bibek Debroy organised a half-day session at the Rajiv Gandhi Institute. Ajay walked Rahul Gandhi and a group of young Congress MPs through pension reform in detail. Amit later points out the irony: the Congress went on to push for a return to the OPS in state after state, even though its leadership had been personally briefed on why it was a disaster.
stories.insight: Knowing the right answer does not determine political behaviour. When incentives point the other way, politicians who know better will still pander.
stories.quote: I did that and, you know, they were interested and they asked all kinds of detailed questions and I explained the whole story to them to the best of my ability.

stories.topic: Surendra Dave vs the Fourteen Insurance CEOs
stories.summary: The insurance industry rebelled against the NPS, arguing that pensions are insurance and that they, not new index-fund managers, should run them. Chidambaram called a meeting with fourteen insurance company CEOs. Ajay was told he could attend but must not speak. Each CEO argued that they knew the business, could do index funds and could even offer guarantees. Chidambaram then turned to Surendra Dave, who gave what Ajay calls a masterly fifteen-minute rebuttal while Ajay's heart was in his mouth. Nobody said anything after. Chidambaram and Dave went off to talk, and later that day word came: the boss has decided, we're doing NPS.
stories.insight: One well-argued rebuttal at the right table can decide a national policy. Defending against incumbents, who would have turned pensions back into defined-benefit products, mattered as much as the design itself.
stories.quote: But Dave's response was absolutely masterly, and nobody said anything.

stories.summary: Chidambaram wanted a law to anchor the NPS and set up the PFRDA as regulator, and UK Sinha led the drafting. But the CPI(M), essential to the UPA-1 coalition, insisted that defined-benefit pensions were 'who we are'. The Congress kept negotiating from 2004 to 2009 and kept going even after 2009 to preserve coalition harmony, finally passing the law in 2013. Meanwhile Chidambaram, whom Ajay calls one of the smartest legal minds in the country, built the regulatory regime out of private contracts. If fund managers or NSDL wanted the business, they had to accept inspections and disclosure. So the NPS ran from 2004, nine years before its law existed.
stories.insight: When legislation is blocked, clever contract design can carry a regulator's load. A brilliant legal mind in government is itself a form of state capacity.
stories.quote: So what would be done in the bill as a regulatory arrangement was done through private contract

stories.topic: 'Your Baradari Is Not Ready': Yashwant Sinha on Inflation Targeting
stories.summary: In 2002 and 2003 Ajay pitched inflation targeting to Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha. Sinha said the idea was too far from conventional Indian economic thinking and that Ajay's community of economists did not yet understand it. Until the broader intellectual consensus shifted, he said, a finance minister could only follow, not lead. Inflation targeting finally arrived in 2015.
stories.insight: Even powerful ministers act within the Overton window set by the intellectual community. Lasting reform comes from shifting what experts broadly accept, not from persuading one official.
stories.quote: Then who am I? I'm a mere finance minister. I can only follow. I can't lead.

stories.topic: The Pension Reform Community That Went Home
stories.summary: Around 1998 to 2004 India had a real pension reform community, with papers, seminars, op-eds and an intellectual ferment that made the NPS possible. Once the decisions were taken, everyone assumed the job was done and the community dissolved. Pension work also moved from KP Krishnan's DEA to the DFS, and institutional memory was lost. Small flaws went unfixed, equity exposure stayed timid, military pensions drifted into OROP, and nobody redid the implicit-debt calculation. When young civil servants began demanding the OPS, Karnataka once informally asked Ajay to spend a day with its trade unions. That kind of patient engagement should have happened everywhere, but there was no one left to do it.
stories.insight: Passing a reform is the start, not the end. Without a standing community to defend and refine it, the field is left to organised interest groups and pandering politicians.
stories.quote: Now, in hindsight, the biggest tragedy was that that community disbanded.

recommendations.reason: It is the founding document of Indian pension reform: defined contributions, individual accounts and cheap index funds.

core_ideas.explanation: A defined benefit (DB) pension guarantees a payout for life, funded in effect by the young paying the old. Every DB payment rests on money coercively taken from someone else, and it pits generations against each other. A defined contribution (DC) pension uses state power only to force you to save into your own account. The money is yours, nobody else can touch it, and nobody pays for anyone else.
core_ideas.quote: The beauty of a defined contribution approach is there is no socialisation, which is the root of all evil.

core_ideas.concept: Why Every DB Pension Blows Up
core_ideas.explanation: Three forces break DB schemes everywhere. Longevity rises, so the value of lifelong payments grows. Birth rates fall, so fewer young people support more old ones. Democratic politics keeps loosening the parameters, such as the pension percentage and the age at which it starts. Ajay is a 'one-handed economist' on this: every DB programme has reneged, or will renege, on its promises.
core_ideas.quote: Every single defined benefit program in the world has got into trouble. There is not one defined benefit program that has stayed out of trouble.

core_ideas.concept: Nominal vs Inflation-Indexed vs Wage-Indexed: Chalk and Cheese
core_ideas.explanation: The three terms sound alike but are completely different creatures. A fixed nominal pension can be funded with sensible planning. Inflation indexing roughly doubles the present value and can only partly be achieved. Wage indexing, which pays you half of what today's workers earn, is astronomically expensive and impossible to fund. Fairness arguments like OROP ('a general retired 20 years ago should get what a newly retired general gets') blow up the numbers.
core_ideas.quote: There does not exist a wise management strategy through which wage indexation can be obtained.

core_ideas.explanation: Life expectancy at birth (about 74 in India) is the wrong number for pensions. Once you survive to 60 or 70, all the earlier ways you could have died are behind you, so your expected remaining life is longer. Pension costs must also use forward-looking longevity, not backward-looking LIC data. Ajay says a 20-year-old today has a reasonable chance of reaching 120.
core_ideas.quote: Once you've made it to 60, you actually have more years to go. Once you've made it to 70, you have more years to go because it's a conditional expectation.

core_ideas.concept: Pensions as a Test of State Capability
core_ideas.explanation: Like waging a war, pension policy is a raw test of whether a state can think. It requires present-value calculations over a hundred years, honest assumptions and the discipline to stay responsible. That is treacherous for a poor country. It ties to defence too: Ajay argues a mighty military is made out of economics, and the first task of Indian military reform is fixing military pensions.
core_ideas.quote: I think of wisdom and sanity on pension policy as a high bar as the test of a state.

core_ideas.concept: Implicit Pension Debt: Stocks vs Flows
core_ideas.explanation: Watching this year's pension payouts (the flow) understates the danger. The real measure is the stock: the present value of all promises already made, equal to the debt you would need to buy annuities for everyone covered. For Indian civil servants that came to 68% of GDP. Ajay says the US figure is 200% of GDP.
core_ideas.quote: Whereas before this work of Gautam Bhardwaj and Surendra Dave, people were looking at the flow of pension payments and they were saying, hey, this stuff is exploding, it's doubling every six years. So this is really scary. But people hadn't appreciated what a big number it turns into that the stock is 68% of GDP.

core_ideas.concept: The NPS: The State Copying Smart Personal Finance
core_ideas.explanation: The NPS makes a civil servant do what a sophisticated saver would do anyway: save, hold equities, use cheap index funds and avoid fees. 20% of salary is deducted into a personal account. A few fund managers chosen by public tender run index funds, where the only test is how little they charge. Choosing by tender is also politically safe, since no one can demand a CBI probe into a manager's performance. An expert committee sets the default mix of equities, corporate bonds and government bonds, but anyone can override it online. NPS Trust holds the money and NSDL keeps the records, and members get an SMS each month as their balance grows.
core_ideas.quote: So the principle, the philosophy of NPS is that can we use the state in creating a mechanism that replicates wise sound behavior of personal finance of a sophisticated person?

core_ideas.explanation: A toxic saying in finance holds that 'fund management is sold, not bought'. It is the logic of celebrity ads, huge commissions and armies of agents pushing tax-saving products on friends and family, which steers money into bad assets. The NPS flips this. Fund managers receive bulk money without even knowing their customers' names, and compete only on price.
core_ideas.quote: There's a phrase in finance which is a deeply toxic one which says that fund management is sold, not bought.

core_ideas.explanation: From the first job until retirement, a pension is simply asset accumulation. It is your money, and your heirs inherit it if you die. Insurance enters only at the end, if you choose to convert your savings into a lifelong monthly annuity. Handing the whole system to insurers would have dragged it back towards defined-benefit thinking.
core_ideas.quote: from age twenty onwards, you're just accumulating assets. It's just fund management. It is not insurance.

core_ideas.concept: Change the Rules at the Point of Recruitment
core_ideas.explanation: The NPS did not take back promises made to existing employees, even those hired a month earlier. Only new recruits joined the new system, and job advertisements said so. That made the reform fair and politically defensible. The OPS revival breaks this logic: recruits who knowingly signed up for the NPS now demand the old promises.
core_ideas.quote: Now you come in with your eyes open. If you don't like it, please don't join the government.

core_ideas.explanation: By design, for about 25 years governments pay both the old pensions and the extra 10% salary that funds new NPS accounts. The fiscal gains only show up around 2029. With no researchers modelling this, politicians saw only the extra cost and lost their nerve just before the payoff. The 25-year wait applies to state finances; individuals in a well-run NPS do better than under the OPS.
core_ideas.quote: And this was done by design that there will be a transition generation where you will pay twice.

core_ideas.concept: Pension Policy Is for the Pensioner: Diversify Globally
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay calls globally diversified equity index funds the closest thing to a free lunch, with global diversification roughly halving risk. His one regret about the NPS design is that it was not globally diversified from day one, with perhaps 60 to 80% of the money invested abroad. Pension money should serve only its owners, not prop up the stock market or fund infrastructure. Timid civil servants also kept equity exposure too low.
core_ideas.quote: If I had to go back in a time machine, I would push that right from the word go, it should have been a globally diversified pool of assets.

core_ideas.concept: Reforms Decay Without an Intellectual Ecosystem
core_ideas.explanation: The OPS revival comes from a small, organised group of civil servants, while the cost falls on everyone. Politicians weigh that group against a non-existent intellectual discourse and pander. The only counterweight is a sustained community of researchers, papers, simulations and op-eds, funded and fed with data. India's last implicit-pension-debt calculation dates to Bhardwaj and Dave.
core_ideas.quote: A country can only be as good as its intellectuals.

core_ideas.concept: Theory of Change: Shift the Overton Window, Don't Whisper in Ears
core_ideas.explanation: A popular theory among Indian philanthropists is to place consultants beside a joint secretary and whisper good ideas. That only produces small changes within what officials already accept. Real reform needs a broad community that changes what is thinkable, as Yashwant Sinha told Ajay about inflation targeting.
core_ideas.quote: The point, however, is to change the Overton window, is to legitimize the complex reforms that are needed in the country that are beyond the horizon of an average policymaker.

core_ideas.concept: The UPS Guarantee Is a Put Option
core_ideas.explanation: The Unified Pension Scheme keeps a fund but promises to top up any annuity below 50% from a guarantee fund. In derivatives terms, that is a put option on the portfolio, and put options can be costly. Its partial inflation indexation also assumes a real (inflation-indexed) annuity market that India does not have. No calculations have been published, so it may become a contingent liability for the state.
core_ideas.quote: So you have a put option on the portfolio that a certain amount of realization will be obtained regardless of what happens to market conditions. And these put options can be pretty expensive.

core_ideas.explanation: Decisions involving sums like 50 to 100% of GDP should come with full calculations, every assumption stated, and code anyone can download and rerun. Ajay and Renuka Sane did this for OROP. He sees it as the only route to a meaningful democratic debate, and the UPS falls short.
core_ideas.quote: So don't take my word for it. And all the assumptions are laid bare.

core_ideas.explanation: Parametric reform keeps the old structure and adjusts its settings, which politics will keep fiddling with forever. Structural reform builds a new system with no dials to turn. The NPS was structural: your money, your account, no fudge factors. NREGS was promised to be self-liquidating, yet its daily wage keeps rising and it distorts the labour market. Ajay fears a government-designed universal healthcare system would creep upward the same way.
core_ideas.quote: In parametric reforms, we hold a basic edifice intact and twiddle with some dials. In structural reform, we create a clean engine and that engine suffers from a lack of those kinds of dials, so it is likely to work better.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit turns the framework on personal life. Locking yourself away for a weekend to write, or sprinting occasionally while unfit, is a parametric tweak. Building daily habits, or changing what and how you eat, is structural. He asks listeners to pause after the episode and ask what is wrong with their lives, and whether it needs a structural or a parametric fix.
core_ideas.quote: We talk here about reforming the state. I tell the reader, reform thyself.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on finally caring about his looks: 'I have always thought I have a face for audio, which is why the Seen and the Unseen Audio Podcast. But since I have started doing the show with you, Ajay, especially given how good looking and dashing you are, I thought I have to make some minimal effort.'

Amit, bleeding and refusing to cancel: 'Man, we gotta shoot. I don't care if I die, but we gotta shoot.' And on his blood-streaked torso: 'Had my torso been a little more better developed, it would have been an exceptionally enticing scene, but it wasn't. It was just bloody.'
Amit: 'Just as this nation is regrettably too full of bleeding heart liberals, here you had a bleeding lip libertarian. Though I do not like labels, Pushpa, so we shall not go there.'
Harry Truman's plea for a 'one-handed economist', one who wouldn't keep saying 'on the other hand'. Ajay calls himself one on defined-benefit pensions, and Amit explains why that certainty is rare.

Amit on wage-indexed pensions: 'After I retire, I want the state to give me every month half of BeerBiceps' income. And we'll be fine. That's where I want it indexed... As far as money is concerned, I'm not doing his content.'
Ajay on the nightmare headline governments fear: 'Oh, this person was a secretary to government and now she's sitting by the gates of the Bangalore Metro begging for a free idli sambar.'
Ajay on pushing cheap index funds in the late 90s against fund-manager machismo ('if you pay peanuts, you will get monkeys'): 'I lost many friends in the financial system.'
Amit imagines a pensions web series with Vajpayee gazing at a young Ajay in his 'languorous, leisurely way'. Ajay deflates it at once: he never sat with Vajpayee on this question.
Ajay on Vajpayee in meetings: 'he had a way of either appearing to be asleep or actually being asleep in meetings. Okay, and you could never tell, but he was a wise man.'
Ajay channelling the insurance lobby: 'We don't want no stinking pension fund managers, we don't want no stinking index funds.'

After Ajay is told to keep quiet in the insurance CEOs' meeting, Amit: 'Gentle reader, this person here who looks like an elder statesman was once a firebrand revolutionary, right? You haven't seen that side of him.'
Ajay on his youthful self at the PFRDA law meetings: 'When I look back, I just think what a dummkopf I was that I didn't understand laws... I would just like nod unintelligently.'

Ajay's dry aside on states trying to grab NPS money: 'last I heard it was not yet easy for governments in India to expropriate our private property. I mean I know they can do it, but it is still hard.'
Ajay inverts Mark Antony's line from Julius Caesar, 26 years after Project Oasis: 'I come to praise the NPS, not bury it.'
Amit invokes 'Jefferson's alleged phrase', eternal vigilance, as the lesson for reformers who go home after a policy passes.
Milton Friedman's matrix of spending, from the public choice episode: the state spends other people's money on other people, so nobody guards the cost of pension promises.
Ajay quotes Bruce Springsteen on India's missing policy intellectuals: 'Well man, the poets around here don't write nothing at all. They just stand by and let it all be.'
Amit quotes Annie Dillard, 'How we spend our days is how we spend our lives', to argue for structural reform through daily habits rather than occasional sprints.
Amit on his diabetes reversal: 'though at the rate I have fallen off the wagon in terms of food, I might well get it back.'

A storm interrupts the outdoor shoot. Amit returns with 'There was a storm. There is a storm', calls the UPS a storm that won't pass easily, and signs off with 'the storm is upon us and we must fight the degradation of the state.' Ajay: 'Does this mean we have to do the next one indoor?'
